name: ThunderMittens
language: C++ (Metal Shading Language) with Python/MLX bindings
baseline: MLX mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention and mx.matmul (Apple's MLX Metal kernels)
workload: The repo's time_attn.py times a forward attention kernel (bf16, head dim 64 and 128, batch 16, 16 heads, sequence 512 to 2560) against mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention, and time_gemm.py times a bf16 square GEMM (1024 to 16384) against mx.matmul, both reported as GFLOPS.
claimed_speedup: No numbers found. The README makes no performance claim and the repo stores no results; the timing scripts only print GFLOPS for 'mlx' and 'tk' side by side (time_attn.py also prints 'diff' as a percentage). The accompanying Hazy Research blog post (hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2024-11-28-tk-mlx) was egress-blocked; a WebSearch snippet for it says only that an M2 Pro has about 200 GB/s memory bandwidth and about 6.5 TFLOPs and that very simple kernels without producer/consumer asynchrony work well there. No speedup figure was visible to me.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Xcode (Metal compiler) for the MSL path, or CMake C++17 with nanobind against MLX for the Python path (kernels/CMakeLists.txt); no optimization flags beyond those defaults.
hardware: Not stated anywhere I could open (Apple Silicon chip unspecified).
stars_or_usage: 24 stars, 7 forks; Metal sibling of the ThunderKittens (HazyResearch) kernel DSL
tradeoffs: Metal Shading Language port of the ThunderKittens tile abstractions: Apple GPUs only, MLX integration through a vendored copy of MLX (ThunderMittens/mlx, MIT, Copyright Apple Inc.). The attention kernel (kernels/attn_fwd/attn_fwd.metal) is bf16 only with head dim 64 or 128 (static_assert) and forward only; the GEMM is a custom bf16 matmul. Early research code with a small kernel set.
caveats: No numeric claim and no stored results, so tier D under the rules (the project is a sibling of widely used ThunderKittens, but is itself small: 24 stars). The repo has no LICENSE file of its own (only the vendored MLX tree carries an MIT license), so the ThunderMittens code is treated as reference-only. The repo history is two commits, both 'revive thundermittens' on 2025-08-26, after the repository had disappeared (ThunderKittens issue #132, 2025-07-02, unanswered). Benchmark script quirks that weaken any future number: in time_attn.py the 'tk' timing loop's warmup calls MLX's SDPA instead of the ThunderMittens kernel, scale=1 is passed to MLX SDPA while the TK kernel call takes no scale, each iteration calls mx.eval (synchronizing launch overhead into the time), and correctness against MLX is not checked in the scripts. A verifier with blog access could find M2 Pro numbers and justify tier C. Opened: the repo page, tree pages, time_attn.py and time_gemm.py via raw.githubusercontent.com (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HazyResearch/ThunderMittens/HEAD/ThunderMittens/kernels/time_attn.py and .../time_gemm.py), attn_fwd.metal, ThunderKittens issue #132; hazyresearch.stanford.edu was EGRESS_BLOCKED.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/HazyResearch/ThunderMittens README; WebSearch 'ThunderMittens ThunderKittens Metal MLX attention GEMM benchmark M2 Pro speedup vs MLX' and 'hazyresearch ThunderMittens blog ThunderKittens on Apple Silicon Metal MLX attention matmul M2 TFLOPs' found only the blog title and hardware-spec snippet, no benchmark numbers

name: KleidiAI (via the llama.cpp KleidiAI backend PR)
baseline: llama.cpp ggml CPU backend's own Arm Q4_0 kernels (master at the time: AArch64 i8mm/dotprod repacked kernels); not XNNPACK, oneDNN or Eigen
workload: llama.cpp prompt processing (pp128) and token generation (tg64) with a llama 1B Q4_0 model (727.75 MiB, 1.24 B params), CPU backend, 1 to 10 threads, KleidiAI I8MM and SME micro-kernels versus llama.cpp master, in llama.cpp PR #11390 (merged 2025-02-20).
claimed_speedup: Mixed, as posted by the PR contributors. Apple M4 Pro, SME kernels, 1 thread: pp128 205.39 t/s vs master 160.94, tg64 62.22 vs 47.84 (about 1.28x and 1.30x, derived from page data); 2 threads: pp 389.43 vs 312.10, tg 99.95 vs 87.31. At 4 threads SME is slower (pp 326.86 vs master 586.83, tg 110.52 vs 157.63) and at 10 threads slower again (pp 435.39 vs 1173.93, tg 162.36 vs 243.65). KleidiAI I8MM path on M4 Pro is about equal or slower (e.g. 4 threads pp 531.04 vs 586.83). Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) I8MM slower in every row (1 thread pp 174.13 vs 181.23); Galaxy A34 pp512 87.11 vs 84.25 but tg128 11.00 vs 13.79. The PR's own summary: 'KleidiAI SME excels with 1-2 threads but degrades significantly at higher core counts. I8MM kernels consistently underperform'.
compiler_and_flags: From the PR (the PR does not say which build produced which table): Apple Clang with 'cmake -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -D GGML_METAL=OFF -D GGML_BLAS=OFF -D GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON -G Ninja'; or LLVM Clang 19.1.7 with CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS='-march=armv9.2a+nosve+sme', -D GGML_NATIVE=OFF -D GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH='armv9.2a+nosve+sme+dotprod+i8mm' -D GGML_OPENMP=OFF. Build 119d3bf.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (SME and I8MM) run by max-krasnyansky; Samsung Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) by the same contributor; Galaxy A34 (8 threads) by rmatif. Exact core configuration beyond thread counts not stated.
stars_or_usage: 187 stars on the GitHub mirror (official source is gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidiai); integrated in llama.cpp (GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI), XNNPACK (open and merged KleidiAI PRs listed on github.com/google/XNNPACK/pulls); ExecuTorch use was named in the task lead and not verified by me
tradeoffs: Arm-only (AArch64; SME/SME2, SVE, i8mm, dotprod variants; will not build on x86). Micro-kernels with caller-controlled output tiling, no threading, no allocation, no dependencies, plain .c/.h pairs (callable from C++); weights must be prepacked (RHS pack) and activations dynamically quantized and packed (LHS pack) per call, so end-to-end gain depends on the framework integration. API may change between releases (two releases per month). Dual license files: Apache-2.0 and BSD-3-Clause in LICENSES/.
caveats: The only numeric comparison I could open is a third-party integration PR from February 2025, and it is not a clean win: faster only for SME at 1-2 threads on M4 Pro, slower at higher thread counts and for the I8MM path on the phones, against llama.cpp's own Arm kernels rather than a library on the project's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen). No XNNPACK-vs-KleidiAI numbers were visible: the open and merged XNNPACK KleidiAI PRs listed titles only, the KleidiAI README and CHANGELOG hold no comparative figures, and the repo's benchmark tool (benchmark/README.md) times KleidiAI variants against each other with placeholder output ('123 ns'). Arm's own published speedup claims (developer.arm.com blogs, ExecuTorch/MediaPipe posts) were not opened. The table values come from WebFetch's page summary; four values (205.39, 160.94, 62.22, 47.84) were cross-checked by a second fetch. Tier B is on the basis of independent contributors, public llama.cpp benchmark tooling, named CPU and build commands; it falls short of A because the PR does not tie each table to one compiler and flag set. KleidiAI has changed substantially since build 119d3bf (e.g. CHANGELOG lists later SME2/SVE GEMV/GEMM kernel improvements), so the numbers are dated; llama.cpp's current docs (docs/build.md) now say the backend selects the best compatible kernel at runtime rather than always using KleidiAI.

name: cuEquivariance
language: Python (frontends; CUDA kernels ship as separate pip packages)
baseline: e3nn (PyTorch equivariant tensor products for MACE, NequIP and similar models)
workload: The repo's PyTorch MACE tutorial (docs/tutorials/pytorch/MACE.rst) contains an executable timing cell comparing e3nn's channelwise tensor product plus scatter_add against cuEquivariance's fused uniform_1d kernel: multiplicity 128 (128x0e + 128x1o), 1000 nodes, 10000 edges, float32, CUDA, 10 throwaway and 1000 timed repetitions with torch.cuda.synchronize.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on any page I could open. The tutorial source prints 'Speedup: {e3nn_avg/cuet_avg}x' at documentation build time but stores no output, and says 'even from this simple example it is clear that cuEquivariance offers a very good speedup for this operation' while noting 'our kernels tend to have best performance for very large input sizes'. CHANGELOG 0.3.0 says '~3x speedup for MACE with cuEquivariance-JAX v0.3.0 compared to cuEquivariance-Torch v0.2.0' and a later entry 'up to 2x speedup in some cases' for uniform 1d kernels; both compare cuEquivariance with its own earlier releases, not with e3nn.
stars_or_usage: 441 stars; NVIDIA library named in the README as accelerating DiffDock, MACE, Allegro and NequIP; JAX examples for MACE and NequIP in cuequivariance_jax/examples
tradeoffs: Python library with PyTorch and JAX bindings. The repository files are Apache-2.0, but the CUDA kernels are installed from separate cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12/cu13 and cuequivariance-ops-jax-cu12/cu13 pip packages; OpenEquivariance's README calls cuEquivariance's kernel package 'closed-source', and I did not find the kernel source or the ops-package license in the repo. NVIDIA-GPU only; beta status per README. Uses the transpose of e3nn's mul_ir data layout and the tutorial warns that layout transposes can be expensive. Triton-based triangle kernels have optional ahead-of-time tuning that can take hours.
caveats: Vendor project, and no vendor number versus e3nn was readable: docs.nvidia.com was EGRESS_BLOCKED and the repo carries only a benchmark cell without output, so the entry is tier D (the project is notable). Even if numbers were found from NVIDIA, vendor evidence would cap at C unless independent. Independent evidence exists in principle: OpenEquivariance's harness (tests/benchmark.py) times cuEquivariance ('cue', 'cue_fused', 'cue_unfused') against e3nn and itself on A100, and its README says OpenEquivariance performs 'on par with the latest version of NVIDIA cuEquivariance', but I did not open numbers from it or from the OpenEquivariance paper (arXiv blocked). Kernel source being closed makes the 'copyable' status partial, hence usability 'mixed'.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuEquivariance README, CHANGELOG.md and docs/tutorials/pytorch/MACE.rst (raw.githubusercontent.com); https://github.com/PASSIONLab/OpenEquivariance README for the closed-source statement

name: OpenEquivariance
language: Python/C++ (JIT-generated CUDA, HIP and SYCL kernels)
baseline: e3nn (torch.compile max-autotune with CUDA graphs in the harness); also compared with NVIDIA cuEquivariance and FlashTP
workload: Clebsch-Gordan tensor products and fused equivariant graph convolutions for MACE, NequIP, DiffDock and e3nn tetris-poly problems, forward and backward, float32 and float64, run by tests/benchmark.py (uvu, uvw, roofline and conv suites; 100 warmup and 100 timed iterations, PRNG seed 11111).
claimed_speedup: README: 'We provide up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn' and performance 'on par with the latest version of NVIDIA cuEquivariance, which has a closed-source kernel package'. Docs (tests_and_benchmarks.rst) and CHANGELOG v0.4.0: 'OpenEquivariance exhibits up to 2x speedup over FlashTP's fused kernels'. No per-problem figures appear on the opened pages; they are in the paper (SIAM ACDA25, arXiv 2501.13986), which was egress-blocked.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (kernels are JIT-compiled at runtime; README asks for PyTorch and GCC 9+).
hardware: NVIDIA A100-SXM-80GB at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory for the paper's benchmarks (docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst); the docs also list V100, A100-40GB, A5000, T4, H100, MI250x and MI300x as run-tested platforms (not benchmarked). CPU not stated.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars, 17 forks; pip package 'openequivariance'; works with MACE and NequIP
tradeoffs: Supports most 'uvu' and 'uvw' e3nn tensor products, not all of e3nn. Results equal e3nn up to rounding for many configurations; for 'uvw' connection modes the weights must be reordered (reorder_weights_from_e3nn/to_e3nn). Fused convolution has an atomics mode that is non-deterministic and a deterministic mode needing receiver-sorted indices plus a transpose permutation. JIT compile at first use; needs a CUDA, HIP or SYCL (beta) toolchain; PyTorch and JAX frontends.
caveats: The headline figures are first-party README statements with no per-problem numbers on the pages I could open, so tier C is a floor. The paper (SIAM ACDA25) is peer reviewed and the benchmark code is public with A100-SXM-80GB stated and exact reproduction commands in docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst, so a verifier with paper access may justify tier B, or A if the paper states compiler and flags. The README sentence is garbled ('up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn perform on par with...'), which is quoted as is. The harness removes e3nn's torch-compile variant for float64 'benzene' because it runs out of memory, and for 'limited-memory' GPUs drops expensive tests. The 2x claim over FlashTP is against FlashTP's fused kernels only. Opened: README, LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md, docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst and tests/benchmark.py via raw.githubusercontent.com, plus the repo tree and commit pages on github.com.

name: SpargeAttn (SpargeAttention)
language: C++ (CUDA) with Python bindings; Triton example
baseline: FlashAttention2 (Figure 2 legend 'FlashAttn'; Table 1 'Full-Attention' does not name the implementation)
workload: Figure 2 (README image): attention kernel speed in TOPS versus sparsity on an RTX 4090, sequence length 22K, head dim 128; Table 1 (assets/exp_table.png): average per-layer attention speed in real generation runs for Llama3.1 (NeedleInAHaystack, 128K), CogVideoX (17K), Mochi (22K), Flux (4.5K) and Stable-Diffusion3.5 (4.5K), reported with accuracy metrics.
claimed_speedup: Table 1, speed in TOPS, Full-Attention vs SpargeAttn (sparsity): Llama3.1 156.9 vs 708.1 (0.54); CogvideoX 166.0 vs 507.9 (0.46); Mochi 164.2 vs 582.4 (0.47); Flux 158.2 vs 280.3 (0.38); StableDiffusion3.5 164.2 vs 293.0 (0.31); ratios about 4.5x, 3.1x, 3.5x, 1.8x and 1.8x (derived from page data). Figure 2 (values read from the chart, approximate): FlashAttn about 165 TOPS flat; SpargeAttn+Sage2 about 410 TOPS at sparsity 0.1 rising to about 875 at 0.6 (about 5.3x, derived); SpargeAttn+FA2 about 370 at 0.6 (about 2.2x over FlashAttn); SageAttention alone about 300. Accuracy in Table 1 stays near the dense baseline (e.g. Llama3.1 WikiText perplexity 6.020 vs 6.013 for full attention).
hardware: RTX 4090 stated for Figure 2; the GPU for Table 1 is not stated in the image.
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; ICML 2025 paper (arXiv 2502.18137); from the SageAttention group (thu-ml)
tradeoffs: Approximate attention: a training-free predicted block-sparse mask (block 128x64) skips work, so the 'topk' parameter trades accuracy for sparsity. The headline numbers stack sparsity on SageAttention's low-bit quantization (SpargeAttn+Sage/Sage2), so part of the gain over FlashAttention2 comes from quantized matmuls, not sparsity (SageAttention alone is about 300 vs FlashAttn about 165 TOPS in Figure 2, read from the chart). CUDA-only (CUDA 12.0+ Ampere, 12.3 Hopper fp8, 12.4 Ada fp8, 12.8 Blackwell), PyTorch 2.3+; older versions required per-model tuning, the recommended API now does not.
caveats: Peer reviewed (ICML 2025) and the numbers sit in the repo as images from the paper (the README states acceptance, and the rendered README shows Figure 2; Table 1 is in assets/exp_table.png, referenced only inside an HTML comment in the README). Short of tier A: no compiler, flags or CPU model, and I found no kernel benchmark script in the repo listing (evaluate/ holds model examples for CogVideoX, Flux, Hunyuan and Wan; tools/ holds gpu_process.py). The README comment says Table 1 and the paper used the SageAttention-based SpargeAttn and that the SageAttention2-based version is about 30% faster, so Table 1 and the current API differ. TOPS for sparse kernels may count only executed or dense-equivalent operations: not stated on the opened pages. The baseline is FlashAttention2, not a library on the project's list. Numbers were read from images using the image viewer; chart values are approximate.

name: FlashAttention-4 (CuTeDSL, Hopper/Blackwell)
baseline: cuDNN 9.13.0 fused attention (also benchmarked: cuDNN 9.19.1.2, Triton 3.6.0, Gluon 3.6.0, FlashAttention 2.8.3)
workload: Attention forward (and backward) in BF16 on B200: head dim 64, 128 and (192,128), causal and non-causal, sequence 1K to 32K with total tokens fixed at 32K, hidden dimension 2048 (32 or 16 heads); TFLOPs/s from 4 * seqlen^2 * head_dim * heads (halved for causal, backward = 2.5x forward).
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: 'up to 1.3x speedup over cuDNN 9.13 and 2.7x over Triton on B200 GPUs with BF16, reaching up to 1613 TFLOPs/s (71% utilization)'; Figure 4 caption: '1.1-1.3x speedup over cuDNN 9.13.0 and 2.1-2.7x over Triton across sequence lengths'. Figure 4 bar labels, head dim 128, non-causal, seq 1K/2K/4K/8K/16K/32K, TFLOPs/s: FA4 1355, 1468, 1532, 1579, 1601, 1613; cuDNN 9.13.0 1157, 1328, 1413, 1460, 1488, 1517 (FA4 about 1.06-1.17x, derived from page data); cuDNN 9.19.1.2 1346, 1474, 1552, 1585, 1609, 1613 (FA4 within about 1.3% either way, derived from page data); Triton 3.6.0 507 to 703; FA2 383 to 432. Causal, head dim 128, 32K: FA4 1576 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 1266 (about 1.24x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1 1540 (about 1.02x, derived); causal 1K: FA4 744 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 717 vs cuDNN 9.19.1 822 (slower).
compiler_and_flags: Per paper Appendix A.1: CUDA 13.1, CuTe-DSL 4.4.1, PyTorch 2.10.0, Triton 3.6, FlashAttention 2.8.3, cuDNN 9.13 and 9.19.1.2; 5 warmup runs then 10 repeats averaged. No nvcc-style flags (CuTe-DSL is JIT compiled).
hardware: NVIDIA B200 (the main text says B200; Appendix A.1 writes 'B100 180GB SXM6 (1000W)', apparently a typo); CPU model not stated.
stars_or_usage: 25.1k stars (whole flash-attention repository, shared with FlashAttention-2 and -3); pip package flash-attn-4; paper by Princeton, Meta, Colfax, NVIDIA, Georgia Tech and Together AI authors, listed in MLSys 2026 proceedings per a WebSearch result
tradeoffs: Written in CuTe-DSL embedded in Python (paper claims 20-30x faster compile than C++ templates), so no C++ build step but a Python/CUTLASS-DSL dependency and JIT compile at first use; Hopper (sm90) and Blackwell (sm100/sm120) only, CUDA 13 recommended for best performance (cu13 extra). Forward and backward, GQA, varlen, paged KV, block sparsity and MLA kernels live in flash_attn/cute. Uses software-emulated exponentials and conditional softmax rescaling (paper abstract), which a numerics-sensitive user should check against a reference softmax.
caveats: The paper's own Figure 4 caption says: 'newer versions of cuDNN have incorporated many of the techniques described in this paper, yielding similar performance to FA4', and the bar labels confirm parity with cuDNN 9.19.1.2 (and cuDNN ahead at short causal sequences). So the 1.1-1.3x lead holds only against cuDNN 9.13.0, the version the authors compared at release. FlashAttention-3 'does not run on B200' (paper footnote), so there is no FA4 versus FA3 comparison on B200, and I found no H100 FA4 numbers in the paper text or README (the README says only 'optimized for Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (e.g. H100, B200)'); the lead asked for FA3/H100 figures, which I could not find. Backward-pass figures (Figures 6 to 8) were not read. Short of tier A because CPU model and flags are not stated, though benchmarks/benchmark_attn.py is public and its defaults (total 32K tokens, 16 heads at head dim 128, 5 warmup, 10 reps, backends fa2/fa3/fa4/cudnn) match the paper's stated settings. The paper was read from the PDF checked into the repo (assets/fa4_paper.pdf); arXiv 2603.05451, the MLSys proceedings page, the Together AI blog and the Colfax post were not opened (EGRESS_BLOCKED). Several authors work on cuDNN or FA4's vendors, so first-party in part, but peer reviewed. Shares a repository with FlashAttention-3 (use id paper:flashattention-4).
